answers.answer: Users struggle most with retrieving photos of milestone moments such as a child’s firsts (first steps, first haircut, first birthday cake smash) and culturally specific occasions (first Holi, Diwali kite play). The difficulty stems from sparse or ambiguous metadata—keywords like "first" or "Holi" are too generic, and the app’s face‑recognition or location filters often mislabel or miss the target image, forcing users to scroll endlessly.

answers.public_feedback: mixed – some public posts echo the difficulty with generic keywords, while others note that the app sometimes mislabels or omits key images

answers.answer: People most reliably recall the visual details of a photo—such as a bright red kite or a frosting‑covered face—alongside who was present and where the moment took place.  Time‑specific cues (exact dates or relative events like “Diwali 2019”) are remembered less often, and only a few participants recall the broader occasion or emotional tone.  Overall, the interview data show that visual content and people are the strongest memory anchors, while time and emotion are weaker.

answers.public_feedback: mixed – public forums and app reviews show lower recall of visual content and people compared to interviews, but agree on the relative importance of time cues.

answers.answer: The participants most often forgot the exact place of the event (4 of 9), followed by the exact date (2 of 9). They also missed the month (1 of 9) and the visual angle of the kite (1 of 9).

answers.answer: When memory is fragmentary, users first translate remembered pieces into keyword searches, then refine with dates, locations, or people. For example, P1 combined a name, place and year into "Anaya park 2019", P3 started with the object "kite" and added colour and date to get "red kite" and "Nov 2019", and P5 turned a vague scene into "playschool 2023" and later "giraffe play school 2022". These queries show a step‑wise build from fragments to precise terms.

[P5] "playschool 2023"

answers.public_feedback: mixed – interviewers use keyword strategies more often than public posts, but natural‑language queries are more common in public feedback.

answers.answer: The search fails most often when the system’s evaluation of the query does not match the user’s mental model—three participants (P1, P5, P6) reported that the app returned many irrelevant or blurry results, forcing them to scroll or abandon the search. One participant (P4) experienced an understanding mismatch, where the app’s generic results did not align with the memory of a specific event. When the search fails, users either refine the query with additional filters (P1, P2), manually scroll through results (P5, P6), or give up and send a substitute photo (P5, P6).

answers.public_feedback: differs – public posts report a much higher share of UNDERSTANDING failures (≈60%) than our sample (≈11%).
